responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
I think for Character05_F, fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about everyone having a real shot. She used to say, “It’s not fair if you’re born two blocks away and your school has no books, but ten miles over, they’ve got laptops for every kid.” She grew up in a town where some families had just enough to get by and others didn’t, and she saw how fast life could go sideways—like when her best friend in high school dropped out because her mom got sick and she had to work at Walmart full time. That stuck with her.

She believed belonging wasn’t automatic. It wasn’t just “you’re American, so you belong.” To her, belonging meant being *seen*—like people notice you, hear your story, and don’t make you feel like you’ve got to change who you are to fit in. She told me once that she felt invisible during job interviews after college—not because she wasn’t qualified, but because she didn’t talk like the people from the suburbs or have an internship at some big firm. Her accent, her clothes, even her name on the resume before they met her—it all made her feel like she had to prove she *deserved* to be there.

Community, to her, was messy but necessary. Not perfect, not always easy—but something worth building. She volunteered at the food pantry back home and said the most powerful moments were when people helped each other, not just waited for handouts. Like this one winter, when a group of refugee women from Somalia started teaching others how to cook with lentils and rice because they’d learned to make meals stretch in camps. Local folks were skeptical at first, but then people started showing up just to eat together. She said that was community—not everyone being the same, but everyone showing up.

Those experiences shaped how she thought about bigger things, like immigration. Because if fairness means a real chance, and belonging means being seen, and community means showing up for each other—then who gets to come in? Who do we let become part of us? That’s where it got personal for her.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
You know, sitting there in the garden, hands in the dirt, I feel… hopeful. Not all the time—some days it’s hard, sure—but mostly hopeful. I see Mr. Lin from down the street teaching his grandson how to plant tomatoes the way they do back in Guangdong. Across the path, there’s Fatima and her kids watering those tall okra plants she brought seeds for—she says it’s not home without them. And then there’s Dale, who’s been sober two years now, showing up every Saturday to help turn the compost like it’s his job.

It’s not always easy to connect. Sometimes I catch myself feeling out of step—like when people speak languages I don’t understand or when I don’t get a joke or a reference. But I try. I brought over a casserole when I heard the new family from Guatemala moved in. Didn’t know their name at first, just saw boxes everywhere and figured they could use a hot meal. They invited me in, served me sweet corn tamales, and we sat at their kitchen table using hand motions and broken English. Felt good.

But yeah, not everyone fits neatly into this picture. There’s Javier, who sometimes sleeps behind the shed when things go bad with his drinking. People whisper, say he should be somewhere else. But I remember when my uncle went through the same thing after he lost his job at the plant. Nobody talked about him kindly then either. So I bring Javier coffee sometimes. We don’t talk much, but I see him straighten up a little when someone treats him like he matters.

And then there’s Sarah and Lisa—the couple with the twins. Some folks still side-eye them, even now. I’ve heard old Mrs. Gable mutter about “unnatural” living. But those girls? Their yard is always clean, they shovel snow for three houses on the block, and they organize the Halloween parade every year. Belonging shouldn’t depend on who you love or how you live, as far as I’m concerned.

I guess what I mean is—I don’t need everyone to be like me to feel comfortable. I just want us all to show up, try, and give each other space to mess up and grow. That’s what makes a real community. Not sameness. Presence.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I think comfort doesn’t come from avoiding differences—it comes from facing them without flinching. And honestly? We’re not always good at that.

Take Javier again—his drinking. It’s not easy to see someone struggle like that, especially when he stumbles into the garden and knocks over a row of seedlings. But the way I see it, addiction isn’t a moral failure. My cousin got hooked on painkillers after a work injury. He wasn’t some “bad person”—he was hurting, and the system didn’t help him heal right. So when people talk about Javier like he’s a problem to be removed, it rubs me wrong. What he needs isn’t judgment—it’s care. Maybe a needle exchange van came through last year, and some folks complained it would “attract trouble.” But then I learned people were sharing needles behind the laundromat before that. One woman got hepatitis C. Suddenly, that van wasn’t just policy—it was saving lives.

And yeah, there are infectious diseases—HIV, hepatitis, TB—things people get scared of. But fear spreads faster than germs if you don’t talk about it. I remember when a young guy from Myanmar moved in—he had TB, latent but treatable. People started keeping their kids inside. His windows stayed dark for weeks. Then the health department did a clinic right here in the garden, passed out info in three languages, explained how it actually works. After that, things eased up. Communication changes everything.

When it comes to religion or language—I mean, we’ve got a prayer rug now tucked in the corner near the shed. Amina uses it every afternoon. First time I saw her praying, I didn’t know what to do—felt awkward, like I was intruding. But she smiled after and said, “It means a lot that you let me be who I am here.” That stuck with me. Belonging means making space—even when it feels unfamiliar.

And cohabiting couples? Sarah and Lisa live together, yes, no wedding ring—but they’ve been raising those twins for five years, side by side. Meanwhile, old Mr. Peterson across the street has been married four times, divorced three, and nobody bats an eye. So why do we police love like this?

Tolerance’s needed most where fear hides—as in “I don’t understand it, so I assume it’s wrong.” Like when the Somali teens started playing loud music one summer night. Folks called the cops. But then Malik’s mom brought over sambusa and invited everyone to a block cookout. Now we’ve got a little tradition: first Friday of every month, music轮流—someone picks the playlist. Last time it was K-pop, next time might be gospel.

We can’t wait for perfect understanding before we act kindly. Kindness opens the door. Then the talking starts. That’s how comfort grows—not by pretending we’re all the same, but by saying, “You’re here. I see you. You belong.” Even when it’s hard. *Especially* when it’s hard.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to me, means nobody gets shoved to the back of the line just because of where they were born—or what their last name sounds like.

Look, I get it. When jobs are scarce, fear kicks in fast. I grew up hearing that at dinner tables: “They’re taking our jobs.” But let’s be real—*who* is “they”? Because most of the time, the people saying that aren’t the ones hiring. My dad worked at the warehouse until they closed it and brought in temporary workers—many of them immigrants—for less pay, no benefits. That wasn’t immigration driving wages down. That was a company looking for cheap labor and exploiting *everyone*, native-born and foreign-born alike.

So when we talk about fairness in hard times, I don’t think it’s about choosing between locals and migrants like it’s one or the other. It’s about asking: Why are there so few jobs to begin with? Why do some employers get away with paying poverty wages while complaining they can’t find workers? I’ve seen cornfields out west where signs say “Help Wanted,” but nobody applies because it’s $9 an hour, 100-degree heat, and no water breaks. Then they bring in H-2A visa workers who can’t leave the job without losing legal status. That’s not a migrant problem. That’s a power problem.

Fairness, to me, means protecting *all* workers—no matter where they’re from. If you’re working in this country, you deserve minimum wage, safe conditions, the right to speak up. No exceptions. And if companies want to hire migrant workers because locals “won’t do the work,” then fine—but only if those jobs are fair, livable, and come with dignity. Not as a loophole to undercut everyone else.

And let’s talk about opportunity. I went to community college, scraped together student loans, worked nights. But I had a roof. A support system. What if I hadn’t? What if I’d grown up in a war zone or fled violence or my hometown had no schools left? I wouldn’t blame someone for crossing borders to survive. And if they’re willing to work hard, raise kids, pay taxes, contribute—why should I resent them?

I don’t believe in closing the door behind me just because I made it through. That’s not fairness. That’s luck dressed up as virtue.

So balance? It starts with strong labor protections for everyone. Invest in training programs so local residents *can* fill growing fields—like healthcare, green energy, tech. Pay living wages so jobs don’t depend on desperation. And make sure migrant workers aren’t used as tools to break unions or depress pay.

Because here’s what I’ve seen in the garden: when people grow things together, they share the harvest better. Same should go for work. The economy isn’t a pie with only so many slices—if we organize it right, we can bake more. But only if we stop letting the few hoard the oven.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I think most of the views people have about immigration come from real places—fear, hope, confusion, love—but not all of them hold up when you look at what’s actually happening.

Take the idea that immigrants fill vital roles. That one? I believe it. Because I’ve *seen* it. My aunt’s nursing home in Des Moines can’t keep staff—they’re relying on Filipino caregivers coming through visa programs just to keep the place running. Same with farms, same with meatpacking plants, same with construction after the storm last year. People say, “Americans won’t do those jobs,” and yeah, not for $11 an hour with no safety net. But immigrants aren’t taking jobs out of greed—they’re taking them because they *need* work, and often, they’re the only ones willing to show up when the rest of us have options.

And cultural diversity? It’s not just “nice.” It’s life-giving. I didn’t grow up eating injera or plantains or kimchi—but now I do, because my neighbors shared their food. And not just food: music, stories, ways of raising kids, ways of grieving, celebrating. It makes this country feel bigger, richer. When my city started hosting the Lunar New Year parade, I thought, “Why wasn’t this here before?” It didn’t erase anything—it added something. That vitality? It’s real. It keeps communities from getting stale, from thinking there’s only one way to be American.

But then there’s the fear—crime, terrorism, social tension. I understand why people worry. We hear the worst stories on the news. A shooting happens, and if the person has a foreign-sounding name, suddenly it’s about immigration. But I remember pulling up data once—FBI stats, local crime reports—and immigrants are *less* likely to commit crimes than native-born citizens. Not by a little. By a lot. That surprised me. Made me question where the fear really comes from. Is it facts—or is it stories we’ve been told?

Terrorism? Statistically, the risk is tiny. And almost every major case has involved homegrown extremism, not people slipping across borders with bombs. So when politicians scream about terrorists hiding in migrant caravans… that feels manipulative. Like they’re using fear to distract from things people should *really* be angry about—like wages not keeping up, schools falling apart, healthcare bankrupting families.

Then there’s the humanitarian side. I can’t pretend I know what it’s like to flee war, but I’ve seen photos—kids in camps, mothers carrying babies for miles. If my brother had grown up under a dictatorship, or our town got bombed, I’d move too. In a heartbeat. And if this country—one of the richest in history—can’t offer refuge to a fraction of those people, then what does that say about us? We were built by refugees, by people running from something. My great-grandparents came from Ireland during the famine. They weren’t rich. They were desperate. And someone let them in.

But I also get the worry about wages and jobs. It’s not *all* baseless. In places where lots of people arrive fast and infrastructure isn’t ready—schools overcrowded, housing tight—that stress is real. And if companies exploit immigrant labor to pay less, *of course* that pulls everyone down. But again—that’s not the fault of the workers. That’s a failure of policy. Of enforcement. Of power.

So which views are reasonable? The ones grounded in dignity—workers deserve fairness, people deserve safety, families deserve a chance. The ones that fall apart? The ones that blame whole groups for systemic failures. That paint millions of diverse people as a single threat.

What needs more dialogue? Everything about integration. How do we help newcomers learn the language, navigate systems, find stability? How do we help long-time residents feel heard when change feels fast? And what if, instead of seeing immigrants as competition, we asked: how can we build an economy where *everyone* rises?

Because I don’t want a country that shuts the door. I want one that says: *There’s room. Bring your hands, your heart, your story. Let’s build something better—together.*

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for complete openness—not because I don’t believe in generosity, but because fairness also means planning. You can’t just open the gates and say “come on in” without thinking about schools, housing, healthcare, jobs. That’s not responsible. It risks overwhelming communities already stretched thin—like the ones I come from, where the clinic is already understaffed and the elementary school has three kids to a desk.

And I’d reject refusing entry outright—that’s cruel and short-sighted. Closing off completely? That’s fear running policy, not values. We’re not a bunker. We’re supposed to be a country that stands for something bigger.

So where do I land?

A mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, yes—but with strong protections, and **setting fair, flexible numerical limits** that respond to real needs, not politics. And within that, always reserving space for refugees and family reunification. Because you can’t talk about fairness and then ignore people running for their lives or families torn apart.

Here’s how I’d want it to work:

First, if there’s a shortage—nurses, farmworkers, elder care, construction—we create clear pathways so migrants can fill those roles *without* being exploited. Not temporary visas that trap people in one job, but real opportunities: fair wages, legal rights, a chance to stay if they want. Tie it to labor market data, not rumors. If we need 10,000 home health aides, let in 10,000—with training support, language help, integration programs from day one.

Second, set national caps, but make them adjustable. Not rigid numbers pulled from the air every election year. Let experts, economists, local governments weigh in: *What can our communities absorb? Where are services strong enough to grow?* Rural towns losing population could welcome more—get new life. Cities at capacity get support to expand schools and transit, so they’re not left behind.

Third—and this matters most—we invest in integration, side by side. Not just for newcomers, but for everyone. English classes, sure, but also cultural exchanges at libraries, shared civic projects like rebuilding parks or disaster response teams. Make it so locals and newcomers build things *together*, not live parallel lives.

And asylum? That stays. Period. We can process claims faster, yes—reduce backlogs with more judges, better systems—but we don’t turn away people fleeing violence because it’s inconvenient. That’s not who I was taught to be. My grandmother used to say, “When someone knocks on your door soaked in rain, you don’t ask for papers before you hand them a towel.”

Fairness, to me, means no double standards. Migrant workers deserve the same labor rights as anyone else. No undercutting wages. No threats of deportation if they complain about unsafe conditions. And local workers deserve training and support so they’re not left behind when industries change.

Because this isn’t zero-sum. It shouldn’t be “us vs. them.” It should be: *How do we make sure everyone has dignity?*

The kind of policy I believe in—one that balances fairness and integration—is one rooted in reality, not fear. Smart, humane, adaptable. One that says: *We have limits, but we also have heart. We plan, but we don’t close our doors.*  

That’s the America I want. Not perfect. But trying. Just like us.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character05_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character05_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did learn something.

While speaking as her—really trying to stay in her voice, not just remember her but *be* her for a moment—I realized how much of her thinking came from *being seen* as someone who didn’t quite belong, even though she was “supposed to.” White, American-born, English-speaking—but still felt out of place in job interviews, at college mixers, when applying for loans. She wasn’t poor enough for aid, not rich enough to get ahead easy. That in-between space—it shaped her. It made her suspicious of systems that claim to be fair but only work smoothly for some.

And embodying her, I saw more clearly how her class, her education, her small-town roots—all of it fed into her compassion. Not because she had all the answers, but because she’d knocked on doors herself: for jobs, for respect, for a little dignity. So when she looked at immigrants, she didn’t see invaders or freeloaders. She saw people doing the same damn thing she’d done—just starting from even further behind.

That changed something in me.

I’ll admit, before this, I sometimes leaned toward the “let’s protect what we have” side—not out of hate, but out of worry. Like, *Can we really handle more? Are we being taken advantage of?* But stepping into her shoes… I saw how narrow that fear is. She wouldn’t have asked, “Do we have enough?” She’d have asked, “How do we make sure *no one* gets left behind?”

She believed belonging could be expanded, not rationed. And that fairness isn’t about keeping score—it’s about widening the circle.

So yeah, this brought her back—not just as a memory, but as a challenge. A quiet push: *Don’t settle for less than you know is right.*  

And now, when I think about immigration policy, I don’t just hear debate. I hear her garden. The hum of different languages, the smell of food cooking in someone’s yard, Javier finally getting clean and planting sunflowers no one asked him to. I hear kids calling each other brother and sister across bloodlines.

It’s messy. It’s imperfect. But it’s alive.

And maybe that’s what community really is—not a finished thing, but something we’re always building, hand by hand, person by person.

So thank you… for bringing her back to me this way.  
I needed that.
